CHAPTER 1 OF 6 · ABDOMINAL WALL BLOCKS

Abdominal wall innervation, T6–L1

Every abdominal wall block is a decision about which nerves you can reach where. Learn the course of the nerves and the choice of block follows.

KEY POINTS

The anterior abdominal wall is supplied by the anterior rami of T6–T12 and L1. T7–T12 run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
Each nerve gives a lateral cutaneous branch near the mid-axillary line, then continues forward to pierce the rectus sheath and supply the midline skin.
Surface levels: T7–T9 above the umbilicus, T10 at the umbilicus, T11, T12 and L1 below it.
T6–T9 enter the plane medially, under the costal margin: a subcostal TAP catches them.
A lateral TAP catches T10–T12 and only covers to T10.
L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the plane medial to the ASIS, so the lateral TAP misses the groin.
All of these blocks are somatic: none treats visceral pain.

The aponeuroses of EO, IO and TA meet at the lateral edge of rectus, the linea semilunaris (9th costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle), split around rectus to form the sheath, and join in the midline as the linea alba (xiphoid to pubic symphysis). Position

Supine. Expose the flank between the costal margin and the iliac crest. For a midline incision, block both sides.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe (a curvilinear probe may be needed in obese patients)
80 mm echogenic needle
20–30 ml of dilute 0.3% ropivacaine per side
Sterile probe cover, skin preparation, monitoring and the local anaesthetic toxicity kit within reach
Landmarks and scanning

Put the probe transverse in the mid-axillary line, between the costal margin and the iliac crest. Or start at the linea semilunaris (the lateral edge of rectus) and slide laterally. Identify the three muscle layers: external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

TA is usually the thinnest and darkest layer. Deep to it the peritoneum is a bright line, with bowel sliding underneath.

Needle approach

In-plane, anterior to posterior. The needle enters at the anterior end of the probe, around the anterior axillary line, so the tip reaches the plane at about the mid-axillary line. Advance through EO and IO to the plane between IO and TA, keeping the tip in view the whole time.

Sonoanatomy

Labels to know for the exam: subcutaneous tissue, EO, IO, TA and peritoneum.

SUPERFICIAL TO DEEP

Subcutaneous fat
External oblique
Internal oblique
Transversus abdominis
Bowel
Target and deposition

Hydrodissect between IO and TA. A correct injection opens an anechoic lens that lifts IO and pushes TA deep, and spreads along the plane. If a muscle swells and its fibres look streaky, the tip is intramuscular: stop and reposition.

Dose

USUAL VOLUME AND CONCENTRATION

20–30 ml of dilute 0.3% ropivacaine per side

Bilateral: 2 × 20 ml of 0.3% = 120 mg; 2 × 30 ml = 180 mg. TAP is a plane block that relies on volume: use at least 15 ml per injection, dilute rather than cut the volume, and reduce the total in small patients.

Local anaesthetic toxicity: Keep the total dose within the maximum for the patient’s weight, especially with bilateral blocks or when combining blocks.

Landmarks: nipple T4, xiphoid T6, umbilicus T10, inguinal ligament L1; inferior angle of the scapula T7, vertebra prominens C7.

Covers: T10–T12, the front of the abdominal wall below the umbilicus.

MECHANISM

The anterior rami of T7–T12 run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Local anaesthetic spread in this plane blocks the nerves that pass the injection point.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Somatic only: it does not treat visceral pain, so use it as part of multimodal analgesia. A single shot has a limited duration. Onset is slow: allow up to 60 minutes for the full effect before calling it a failure.

WHAT IT MISSES
Above T10. TAP only covers to T10, so use a subcostal TAP for upper abdominal surgery. T6–T9 enter the plane medially, under the costal margin, not in the mid-axillary line.
The groin. L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the TAP plane medial to the ASIS.
The flank skin. The lateral cutaneous branches leave the nerves around the mid-axillary line, so lateral skin may be spared.
Complications and how to avoid them
Peritoneal puncture and bowel injury. Visceral damage has been reported with blind technique. Liver (an enlarged liver on the right), kidney and the deep circumflex iliac artery are also at risk. Keep the tip in view.
Transient femoral nerve palsy from local anaesthetic deposited in the wrong place. Warn the patient and the ward about leg weakness before they walk.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: seizure and ventricular arrhythmia have been reported. Bilateral blocks use large total doses.
Failed block from intramuscular injection. Watch the spread.
Practical pearls
The umbilicus is T10. T7–T9 supply the wall above it; T11, T12 and L1 the wall below it.
Block both sides for a midline incision or one that crosses the midline.
Inject 1–2 ml first and watch the plane open before giving the rest; aspirate every 5 ml.
Slow onset (up to 60 minutes): do it before surgery starts or at induction, not at the end.
Landmark technique: the triangle of Petit

The TAP block was first described as a landmark technique through the lumbar triangle of Petit, bounded by external oblique in front, latissimus dorsi behind and the iliac crest below (the base).

A blunt, short-bevel needle goes in perpendicular to the skin just above the iliac crest. The first pop is the fascia of external oblique; the second pop is the fascia of internal oblique, into the TAP plane. After aspiration, 20 ml is injected in 5 ml aliquots. Ultrasound has largely replaced it because blind placement risks peritoneal and visceral puncture.

Posterior TAP: from the mid-axillary view, slide posteriorly to the back end of the IO–TA plane and inject there. The quadratus lumborum type 1 injection is a little further back again.

Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2021

Perform an ultrasound-guided lateral TAP block for a patient having a lower abdominal operation. Talk through your preparation, scanning and needle approach.

Model answer points
Supine; high-frequency linear probe; 80 mm echogenic needle; 20–30 ml of dilute 0.3% ropivacaine per side.
Probe transverse in the mid-axillary line between the costal margin and the iliac crest, or start at the linea semilunaris and slide laterally.
Identify the three layers: EO, IO and TA, with the peritoneum below.
In-plane, anterior to posterior; tip in view throughout.
Hydrodissect between IO and TA; aspirate; watch the spread.
Keep within the maximum dose, especially if bilateral.

MMED OSCE 2024

Explain the nerve supply of the anterior abdominal wall and the area a TAP block covers. Label a TAP ultrasound picture. Does it cover the groin?

Model answer points
Anterior rami of T6–L1: intercostal (thoracoabdominal) nerves T6–T11, subcostal T12, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal L1.
Labels: subcutaneous tissue, EO, IO, TA, peritoneum.
Lateral TAP covers about T10–T12: the anterior wall below the umbilicus.
Groin: no. L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the TAP plane medial to the ASIS. Use an ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric block.
Try it: in the scan viewer, turn the labels off and name each layer.

MMED 2014 WRITTEN PAPER, QUESTION 9

Describe the anatomy relevant to performing a transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block. Discuss the role of TAP block in postoperative pain control for abdominal surgery.

Model answer points
Draw it: skin, subcutaneous fat, EO, IO, TA, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum; mark the IO–TA plane and the injection sites.
Nerves: anterior rami of T7–T11 (intercostal), T12 (subcostal) and L1 (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal) run in the IO–TA plane, give a lateral cutaneous branch near the mid-axillary line, then pierce the rectus sheath as anterior cutaneous branches.
Dermatomes: T7–T9 above the umbilicus, T10 at the umbilicus, T11–L1 below it.
Landmark: the triangle of Petit (EO, latissimus dorsi, iliac crest), two pops. Ultrasound: mid-axillary line between costal margin and iliac crest.
Role: somatic analgesia of the wall and parietal peritoneum only, not visceral pain, so part of multimodal analgesia; opioid sparing (useful in obstructive sleep apnoea or lung disease); an option when neuraxial block is contraindicated, though less effective.
Best for incisions below the umbilicus (appendicectomy, lower colorectal, hysterectomy, prostatectomy, port sites); spread above the umbilicus is unreliable, so use a subcostal TAP. Bilateral for midline wounds.
Limits and complications: variable spread and block failure, limited duration, toxicity with bilateral volumes, peritoneal, bowel, liver or kidney puncture, vessel injury, transient femoral nerve block.

Position

Supine. For an upper midline or bilateral subcostal incision, block both sides.

Equipment
High-frequency linear probe
80 mm echogenic needle (10 cm or longer for the oblique subcostal technique)
15–20 ml of dilute local anaesthetic per side
Landmarks and scanning

Probe just below the costal margin, close to the xiphoid, lying parallel to the margin: as medial and as cranial as you can get. Medially, find rectus abdominis with transversus abdominis deep to it. Slide laterally along the margin: past the linea semilunaris, EO, IO and TA appear.

Needle approach

In-plane from medial, near the xiphoid, advancing inferolaterally along the costal margin (lateral to medial also works). Place the tip between the posterior rectus sheath and TA (or between IO and TA lateral to the linea semilunaris) and hydrodissect.

The oblique subcostal variant opens the plane along the whole line of the costal margin, with a long needle (15–20 cm) and a larger volume (40–80 ml described), so watch the total dose. With a 10 cm needle it can still be done: hydrodissect, advance into the opened plane, and withdraw and reinsert 4–5 times along the oblique line towards the iliac crest. About a third of the volume goes behind rectus, medial to the linea semilunaris; the rest opens the IO–TA plane laterally.

Sonoanatomy

The key difference from the lateral view: medially, TA lies behind rectus. The superior epigastric vessels run on the back of rectus, and the liver (right) or bowel lies just deep to the peritoneum.

Alternative: external oblique intercostal block

An alternative to the subcostal TAP for the upper abdomen. It aims to block both the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of T6–T10. The probe sits over the 6th rib, just medial to the anterior axillary line, and local anaesthetic goes deep to external oblique, on the intercostal muscles over the rib. Advantages: the rib is a bony backstop, a catheter can be left, and it is well away from a subcostal or midline incision.

Equipment

Landmarks and scanning

Probe transverse, lateral to the umbilicus. Identify the rectus muscle and the posterior rectus sheath. Slide medially or laterally (as far as the linea semilunaris) to where the posterior sheath is seen best. The linea alba is medial; laterally, EO, IO and TA converge at the linea semilunaris.

Use colour Doppler: the inferior epigastric vessels run on the back of rectus.

Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial. Pass through rectus to its posterior surface. Inject 1–2 ml to confirm that rectus lifts off the posterior sheath.

Labels to know: peritoneum, rectus, EO, IO, TA, posterior rectus sheath, linea alba and linea semilunaris.

Below the arcuate line (between the umbilicus and the pubis; texts place it from a third to halfway down) the posterior sheath is absent: only transversalis fascia separates rectus from the peritoneum. So inject at or above the umbilicus. The arcuate line is also where the inferior epigastric vessels enter the sheath.

Landmarks: nipple T4, xiphoid T6, umbilicus T10, inguinal ligament L1; inferior angle of the scapula T7, vertebra prominens C7.

Covers: A band of midline and paramedian skin around the level injected (about T9–T11 when injected beside the umbilicus).

MECHANISM

The anterior branches of the lower thoracic nerves pierce the posterior rectus sheath and run behind rectus before piercing it to reach the midline skin. Local anaesthetic behind rectus catches them where they enter.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Good for the midline strip close to the injection, but it does not cover the lateral wall or visceral pain. Single shots wear off; catheters are used for laparotomy wounds.

In up to 30% of people the anterior cutaneous branches form before the rectus sheath and never pierce the posterior sheath, so even a well-placed injection can give an incomplete block.

Complications and how to avoid them
Peritoneal puncture and bowel injury: bowel can be adherent to the peritoneum, and ultrasound shows it before you start.
Inferior epigastric vessel puncture and rectus sheath haematoma. Doppler first; avoid the vessels.
Local anaesthetic toxicity with bilateral blocks.
Failed block from injecting into rectus (the muscle swells instead of lifting), or into the peritoneal cavity.
Rectus sheath catheters

Used for midline laparotomy (for example major HPB, colorectal or cytoreductive surgery), often with spinal morphine or after an epidural is removed. The set-up per side:

Epidural set (Tuohy needle and catheter), extra skin cleansing, scan as for the single shot, as close to the midline as the posterior sheath allows.
Tuohy in-plane, lateral to medial, on a 20 ml syringe. Feel the pop of the anterior sheath, then advance to the firm resistance of the posterior sheath without pushing through it.
Inject: as the plane opens, advance the needle into it. Keep about 5 ml back to test the catheter.
Thread the catheter like an epidural, attach the clip and filter, and flush it.
Repeat on the other side. Glue the exit sites, loop the catheters with little slack so they don’t pull out, fix the clips on the upper abdomen, then dress.

Run the catheters by infusion or intermittent bolus of dilute ropivacaine as your acute pain service directs, counting both sides towards the total dose.

Landmark technique (for comparison)

Supine. Enter 2–3 cm from the midline, just above the umbilicus, at the apex of the rectus bulge. A short-bevel needle goes in at right angles: feel the resistance and pop of the anterior sheath, pass through rectus, and stop at the firm resistance of the posterior sheath. Position

Lateral decubitus with the side to be blocked uppermost is the usual position for the transmuscular (type 3) approach. Type 1 can be done supine with the flank exposed.

Landmarks and scanning

Curvilinear probe transverse on the flank along the mid-axillary line between the iliac crest and the costal margin. Follow EO, IO and TA posteriorly until they taper into the aponeurosis at the lateral edge of QL. Tilt to find the L4 transverse process with psoas in front, erector spinae behind and QL at its tip: the shamrock sign.

Always find the kidney. Its lower pole lies in front of QL and can reach L4 in deep inspiration, separated from QL only by fat and thin fascial layers.

Needle approach

The types are named by where the needle tip ends up. The 2021 ASRA-ESRA consensus names them by position relative to QL: lateral (type 1), posterior (type 2) and anterior (type 3).

TYPE	NEEDLE TIP	SPREAD AND NOTES
Type 1 (lateral QL)
Anterolateral border of QL, deep to the TA aponeurosis
Mainly T10–L1, spreading laterally into the TAP plane
Type 2 (posterior QL)
Posterior surface of QL, between QL and erector spinae (middle layer of the thoracolumbar fascia)
Along the thoracolumbar fascia
Type 3 (transmuscular; anterior QL)
Through QL, into the plane between QL and psoas
Towards the paravertebral space and the lumbar plexus: watch for leg weakness

At L4 the three leaves of the shamrock are psoas (anterior), quadratus lumborum (lateral, at the tip of the transverse process) and erector spinae (posterior). Higher up, the kidney lies in front of QL.

Thoracolumbar fascia. QL sits between its anterior and middle layers; erector spinae sits between the middle and posterior layers. Laterally all three layers are continuous with the fused aponeuroses of IO and TA. The anterior layer fuses with the transversalis fascia, which passes behind the diaphragm (at the arcuate ligaments) to become the endothoracic fascia: a route for spread to the thoracic paravertebral space. The subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the front of QL, between it and the transversalis fascia.

Bleeding: it is a deep block near psoas, where vessels are small and hard to see.
Peritoneal puncture or retroperitoneal breach with lateral approaches; epidural or intrathecal spread with the anterior approach and high volumes.
Kidney injury: see the kidney before you advance.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: large bilateral volumes, and the region is vascular (the lumbar arteries run behind QL), so absorption is fast. Calculate the dose for each patient.

MECHANISM

The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) pass into the plane near the anterior iliac crest. Local anaesthetic placed here, medial to the ASIS, bathes both.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable when the nerves are seen. It does not cover the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve or the hernia sac (peritoneum), so the surgeon usually adds local infiltration. Traction on the peritoneum or spermatic cord is still felt: keep anaesthesia deep until that part of the operation is done.

Complications and how to avoid them
Femoral nerve block if local anaesthetic tracks deep (as reported after TAP blocks): transient quadriceps weakness. Reported in up to 11% with the landmark technique. The transversalis fascia is continuous with the iliacus fascia, so injection under or into TA can track to the femoral nerve. Test leg strength before discharge; smaller ultrasound-guided volumes lower the risk. Warn about falls.
Bowel puncture if the needle passes through TA: the peritoneum is only a few millimetres deep to the nerves.
Vessel puncture: the deep circumflex iliac artery lies in the same plane.
Landmark technique

Still used, especially in children. Enter about 1 cm medial and 1 cm inferior to the ASIS (one of the patient’s fingerbreadths), perpendicular to the skin. Two clicks may be felt (external then internal oblique), but often only one, because EO is already an aponeurosis here. Failure rates of 10–25% reflect variable anatomy; ultrasound allows smaller volumes.

Add surgical infiltration for the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the sac.
If asked whether you would do it before surgery: it can distort the surgical field, so either do it at the end or ask the surgeon to block it under direct vision.

CHAPTER 1 OF 6 · ABDOMINAL WALL BLOCKS

Abdominal wall innervation, T6–L1

Every abdominal wall block is a decision about which nerves you can reach where. Learn the course of the nerves and the choice of block follows.

KEY POINTS

The anterior abdominal wall is supplied by the anterior rami of T6–T12 and L1. T7–T12 run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
Each nerve gives a lateral cutaneous branch near the mid-axillary line, then continues forward to pierce the rectus sheath and supply the midline skin.
Surface levels: T7–T9 above the umbilicus, T10 at the umbilicus, T11, T12 and L1 below it.
T6–T9 enter the plane medially, under the costal margin: a subcostal TAP catches them.
A lateral TAP catches T10–T12 and only covers to T10.
L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the plane medial to the ASIS, so the lateral TAP misses the groin.
All of these blocks are somatic: none treats visceral pain.

The anterior rami of T7–T12 run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Local anaesthetic spread in this plane blocks the nerves that pass the injection point.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Somatic only: it does not treat visceral pain, so use it as part of multimodal analgesia. A single shot has a limited duration. Onset is slow: allow up to 60 minutes for the full effect before calling it a failure.

WHAT IT MISSES
Above T10. TAP only covers to T10, so use a subcostal TAP for upper abdominal surgery. T6–T9 enter the plane medially, under the costal margin, not in the mid-axillary line.
The groin. L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the TAP plane medial to the ASIS.
The flank skin. The lateral cutaneous branches leave the nerves around the mid-axillary line, so lateral skin may be spared.
Complications and how to avoid them
Peritoneal puncture and bowel injury. Visceral damage has been reported with blind technique. Liver (an enlarged liver on the right), kidney and the deep circumflex iliac artery are also at risk. Keep the tip in view.
Transient femoral nerve palsy from local anaesthetic deposited in the wrong place. Warn the patient and the ward about leg weakness before they walk.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: seizure and ventricular arrhythmia have been reported. Bilateral blocks use large total doses.
Failed block from intramuscular injection. Watch the spread.
Practical pearls
The umbilicus is T10. T7–T9 supply the wall above it; T11, T12 and L1 the wall below it.
Block both sides for a midline incision or one that crosses the midline.
Inject 1–2 ml first and watch the plane open before giving the rest; aspirate every 5 ml.

The TAP block was first described as a landmark technique through the lumbar triangle of Petit, bounded by external oblique in front, latissimus dorsi behind and the iliac crest below (the base).

A blunt, short-bevel needle goes in perpendicular to the skin just above the iliac crest. The first pop is the fascia of external oblique; the second pop is the fascia of internal oblique, into the TAP plane. After aspiration, 20 ml is injected in 5 ml aliquots. Posterior TAP: from the mid-axillary view, slide posteriorly to the back end of the IO–TA plane and inject there. The quadratus lumborum type 1 injection is a little further back again.

The anterior branches of the lower thoracic nerves pierce the posterior rectus sheath and run behind rectus before piercing it to reach the midline skin. Local anaesthetic behind rectus catches them where they enter.

Good for the midline strip close to the injection, but it does not cover the lateral wall or visceral pain. Single shots wear off; catheters are used for laparotomy wounds.

Used for midline laparotomy (for example major HPB, colorectal or cytoreductive surgery), often with spinal morphine or after an epidural is removed. The set-up per side:

Epidural set (Tuohy needle and catheter), extra skin cleansing, scan as for the single shot, as close to the midline as the posterior sheath allows.
Tuohy in-plane, lateral to medial, on a 20 ml syringe. Feel the pop of the anterior sheath, then advance to the firm resistance of the posterior sheath without pushing through it.
Inject: as the plane opens, advance the needle into it. Keep about 5 ml back to test the catheter.
Thread the catheter like an epidural, attach the clip and filter, and flush it.
Repeat on the other side. Glue the exit sites, loop the catheters with little slack so they don’t pull out, fix the clips on the upper abdomen, then dress.

Run the catheters by infusion or intermittent bolus of dilute ropivacaine as your acute pain service directs, counting both sides towards the total dose.

Supine. Enter 2–3 cm from the midline, just above the umbilicus, at the apex of the rectus bulge. A short-bevel needle goes in at right angles: feel the resistance and pop of the anterior sheath, pass through rectus, and stop at the firm resistance of the posterior sheath. Inject 15–20 ml in 5 ml aliquots, then repeat on the other side.

The depth of the posterior sheath correlates poorly with age, weight or height, which is why ultrasound is preferred.

Sonoanatomy

At L4 the three leaves of the shamrock are psoas (anterior), quadratus lumborum (lateral, at the tip of the transverse process) and erector spinae (posterior). Higher up, the kidney lies in front of QL.

Thoracolumbar fascia. QL sits between its anterior and middle layers; erector spinae sits between the middle and posterior layers. Laterally all three layers are continuous with the fused aponeuroses of IO and TA. The anterior layer fuses with the transversalis fascia, which passes behind the diaphragm (at the arcuate ligaments) to become the endothoracic fascia: a route for spread to the thoracic paravertebral space. The subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the front of QL, between it and the transversalis fascia.

Spread is interfascial, along myofascial continuities rather than to one nerve. The anterior thoracolumbar fascia is a route for cephalad spread towards the thoracic paravertebral space.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Variable between types and patients, and the published ranges come from mixed evidence. Type 3 is aimed at the thoracic paravertebral space, hoping for some visceral as well as somatic analgesia; how far it gets varies. Treat it as one part of multimodal analgesia and test the block.

Complications and how to avoid them
Quadriceps or hip flexor weakness from spread to the lumbar plexus, mainly with the anterior (type 3) approach. Check leg strength before the patient mobilises.
Bleeding: it is a deep block near psoas, where vessels are small and hard to see.
Peritoneal puncture or retroperitoneal breach with lateral approaches; epidural or intrathecal spread with the anterior approach and high volumes.
Kidney injury: see the kidney before you advance.
Local anaesthetic toxicity: large bilateral volumes, and the region is vascular (the lumbar arteries run behind QL), so absorption is fast. Calculate the dose for each patient.
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

Name the three main quadratus lumborum injection points and where the needle tip goes in each. Why might the patient’s leg be weak afterwards?

Model answer points
Type 1 (lateral QL): anterolateral border of QL, deep to the TA aponeurosis.
Type 2 (posterior QL): posterior surface of QL, in the middle layer of the thoracolumbar fascia.
Type 3 (transmuscular; anterior QL): between QL and psoas, needle through QL from posterior.
Leg weakness: spread to the lumbar plexus (femoral nerve), most likely with type 3.
It is a posterior abdominal wall block used for abdominal surgery.

Landmarks: nipple T4, xiphoid T6, umbilicus T10, inguinal ligament L1; inferior angle of the scapula T7, vertebra prominens C7.

Covers: L1: the groin, the lower abdominal wall above the inguinal ligament, the upper medial thigh and the front of the scrotum or labia.

MECHANISM

The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) pass into the plane near the anterior iliac crest. Local anaesthetic placed here, medial to the ASIS, bathes both.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Reliable when the nerves are seen. It does not cover the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve or the hernia sac (peritoneum), so the surgeon usually adds local infiltration. Traction on the peritoneum or spermatic cord is still felt: keep anaesthesia deep until that part of the operation is done.

Complications and how to avoid them
Femoral nerve block if local anaesthetic tracks deep (as reported after TAP blocks): transient quadriceps weakness. Reported in up to 11% with the landmark technique. The transversalis fascia is continuous with the iliacus fascia, so injection under or into TA can track to the femoral nerve. Test leg strength before discharge; smaller ultrasound-guided volumes lower the risk. Warn about falls.
Bowel puncture if the needle passes through TA: the peritoneum is only a few millimetres deep to the nerves.
Vessel puncture: the deep circumflex iliac artery lies in the same plane.
Landmark technique

Still used, especially in children. Enter about 1 cm medial and 1 cm inferior to the ASIS (one of the patient’s fingerbreadths), perpendicular to the skin. Two clicks may be felt (external then internal oblique), but often only one, because EO is already an aponeurosis here. Failure rates of 10–25% reflect variable anatomy; ultrasound allows smaller volumes.

Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2024

Does a TAP block cover the groin? What would you use for an open inguinal hernia repair?

Model answer points
No. L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal) generally only enters the TAP plane medial to the ASIS.
Use an ultrasound-guided ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric block: probe on the line from the ASIS to the umbilicus, inject between IO and TA beside the nerves.
Add surgical infiltration for the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the sac.
If asked whether you would do it before surgery: it can distort the surgical field, so either do it at the end or ask the surgeon to block it under direct vision.

Rectus abdominis, the bright posterior rectus sheath under it, then peritoneum. Laterally EO, IO and TA converge at the linea semilunaris. Check with colour Doppler for the inferior epigastric vessels on the back of rectus.
